summary: Defines new parameters and encodings for the OAuth 2.0 token and introspection endpoints when used with the ACE framework. They express the proof-of-possession key the client wants, the one the authorization server picked, and the one the resource server uses to authenticate to the client.

eli5.summary: This adds boxes on the permission form for naming which key proves who holds the permission.

questions: ace proof of possession key parameters
subtitle: Three small parameters that say which key an ACE access token is bound to, and which key the resource server uses.

tldr.problem: The ACE framework needs a way for a client to ask for a specific proof-of-possession key, for the authorization server to name the key it chose, and for the resource server's own public key to reach the client.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9201 defines req_cnf for the token request, cnf for the token and introspection responses, and rs_cnf for the resource server's public key. Their values follow the cnf claim syntax, and CBOR keys 4, 8 and 41 are assigned.
tldr.outcome: The parameters live in their own document so they can be reused outside RFC 9200. All security and privacy considerations of RFC 9200 apply.

today: RFC 9201 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is meant to be used together with RFC 9200, though the parameters can also be used independently of it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The ACE framework in RFC 9200 needs new parameters for the OAuth 2.0 token and introspection endpoints, and new claims for access tokens. RFC 9201 puts them in a dedicated document so they can also be used independently of RFC 9200.

The examples use the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), but JSON MAY be used as an alternative for HTTP-based communications, as specified in RFC 9200. Key terms such as client, resource server and authorization server come from RFC 9200, and examples use the COSE_Key structure.
sections.eli5: The new form boxes were written in their own little booklet so other people can use them too, not just the original ACE users.

sections.title: Token Endpoint Parameters
sections.content:
In the client's request, req_cnf is OPTIONAL and carries the key the client wants bound to the token for proof of possession. It is RECOMMENDED that an AS rejects a request containing a symmetric key value, since the AS can generate better symmetric keys than a constrained client. This does not apply to key identifiers that reference a symmetric key. The AS MUST verify that the client really holds the key, and profiles that allow req_cnf MUST define the proof-of-possession method.

In the AS response, cnf is REQUIRED if the token type is pop and a symmetric key is used, and MAY be present for asymmetric keys. It holds the key the AS selected. The rs_cnf parameter is OPTIONAL when the token type is pop and asymmetric keys are used, and MUST NOT be present otherwise. It carries the public key the RS uses to authenticate. If it is absent, either the RS uses no public key or the AS knows the RS can authenticate itself without extra information.

All three take the syntax and semantics of the cnf claim, from RFC 8747 for CBOR or RFC 7800 for JSON.
sections.eli5: One box says which key you would like, another says which key the office picked, and a third shows the door's own key so you know you are at the right door.

sections.title: Introspection and Usage Rules
sections.content:
For introspection, RFC 9201 defines CBOR instead of JSON for the cnf response parameter from RFC 8705. When CBOR is used, the AS MUST use the mapping in the CBOR table and the value follows the cnf claim syntax of RFC 8747. In an introspection response from the AS to the RS, cnf is REQUIRED if the token is a proof-of-possession token and absent otherwise.

In a token response, cnf is OPTIONAL for an asymmetric key or a key the client named by identifier, and REQUIRED if the client sent no req_cnf and symmetric keys are used. The rs_cnf parameter is OPTIONAL and indicates the RS's public key when the key-to-identity binding is not established otherwise.

If a COSE_Key contains an alg or key_ops parameter, the client MUST NOT use a key incompatible with the profile or algorithm. An RS MUST reject such a proof with a response equivalent to CoAP 4.00 (Bad Request). If a token's audience includes several RSs, rs_cnf MUST NOT be used, since the client cannot tell which RS the key belongs to.
sections.eli5: The door guard learns which key goes with the pass. If a key is labeled for a different use, it must not be used, and if one pass opens many doors, no single door key can be shown.

sections.title: CBOR Mappings and Key Rules
sections.content:
When CBOR is used, the new names map to integer keys: req_cnf is 4 in a token request, cnf is 8 in both the token response and the introspection response, and rs_cnf is 41 in the token response. All three have a map as their value type.

One extra rule covers asymmetric keys. An RS that authenticates to the client with asymmetric keys MUST NOT hold several different key pairs applicable to the same authentication algorithm, for example several pairs for the same DTLS cipher suite. The RS cannot tell which key to use before the client's identity is established, so attempts could randomly fail unless algorithm negotiation gives a unique choice.
sections.eli5: Each box gets a short number so messages stay small. And a door should only have one key of each kind, or the guard might grab the wrong one.

sections.title: Security, Privacy and Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 9201 is an extension of RFC 9200 and says that all security considerations and all privacy considerations from that document apply here as well. It adds no new ones of its own.

IANA is asked to register req_cnf, rs_cnf and cnf in the OAuth Parameters registry. It also registers the CBOR mappings (4, 8 and 41) in the OAuth Parameters CBOR Mappings registry, and the cnf mapping in the OAuth Token Introspection Response CBOR Mappings registry.
sections.eli5: Everything about staying safe and private is already in the main rulebook, so this booklet just points back to it.
